title: Saving for a Home
summary: Work out the full cash you need for a home in four funds, build a savings route and test the timeline.
subtitle: Build the entire purchase fund before the listing photos start making decisions

blocks.text: Reaching the minimum down payment feels like the summit. Then closing costs, moving expenses and the emergency reserve arrive carrying clipboards.

This lesson builds a complete home-purchase cash target instead of treating the down payment as the whole trip. You will work out four separate funds, compare savings routes and record where the money came from. You will also pick a timeline that leaves the household steady after you move in. Mortgage approval, tax eligibility and provincial purchase costs need to be checked separately. This workbook organizes your preparation.

For homes priced from more than $500,000 to less than $1.5 million, the current federal minimum is 5% of the first $500,000 plus 10% of the portion above $500,000. At $1.5 million or more, the minimum is 20%.

items.title: “Once I save the down payment, I am financially ready to buy.”
items.text: A buyer also needs money for closing costs, moving and first repairs, plus a reserve that lasts past the purchase. Qualifying for a mortgage and affording the home are separate tests.

blocks.text: The down payment is the summit everyone photographs. Closing, move-in and the reserve are the rest of the mountain.
blocks.detail: Giving every dollar its own labelled fund keeps a correct down-payment number from becoming an incomplete plan.
blocks.extra: Four funds to build start now, before a single showing gets booked.

blocks.text: FCAC suggests planning about 1.5% to 4% of the purchase price for upfront or closing costs. On $550,000, that is an illustrative $8,250 to $22,000 before moving and reserves.

items.text: FHSA: Current CRA rules give $8,000 of room in the first year an eligible person opens an FHSA, with a $40,000 lifetime limit on contributions or transfers. Contributions are generally deductible. Qualifying withdrawals may be tax-free.
Home Buyers’ Plan: An eligible person may currently take up to $60,000 out of RRSPs under the HBP. You generally repay it over up to 15 years. Missed repayments may be added to your income.
TFSA: Available room may support flexible tax-free saving and withdrawals. Confirm your contribution room, and remember that room you withdraw normally comes back in a later year.

Accessible savings or GICs: For a near or known purchase date, compare access, maturity dates, penalties, rates and deposit protection. Do not make the closing fund depend on a last-minute market recovery.

blocks.text: CRA allows an HBP withdrawal and an FHSA withdrawal for the same home, if you meet every condition for each program.

items.title: “FHSA and HBP money is automatically tax-free for every first-home purchase.”
items.text: Who qualifies, the limits, the qualifying-home rules, withdrawal timing and HBP repayments all matter. Check the current CRA requirements before moving money.

sections.title: Sophie and Marcus Meet the Second Mountain

paragraphs: Sophie Tremblay and Marcus Reed have saved $30,000 toward a $550,000 home near Ottawa. They open the savings app, admire the round number and book three showings. In their minds, the down payment flag is already planted at the summit. The other costs, apparently, will hike up on their own.

Then their mortgage professional asks three questions. How much cash is set aside for closing? Where did two large deposits come from? What will be left after they get the keys? Their down payment math is right. But they have not saved for legal and inspection costs, property-tax adjustments, moving or repairs. One deposit is a family gift with no paperwork. Another has travelled through so many accounts that it looks more mysterious than it deserves.

Sophie and Marcus build a four-part target. The $30,000 down payment stays separate. They use FCAC’s percentage range to set a closing-cost band, price the move and set a reserve that stays untouched after closing. They check their FHSA room and withdrawal rules, look at Marcus’s possible HBP use and repayment, and confirm each step with the institutions and current CRA guidance.

The full target is bigger than $30,000. They could cover the gap on credit cards. They don’t. They lower the price they are shopping for, add ten months to the timeline and set up automatic transfers on each payday. The family gift gets its paperwork before it joins the fund. Statements go in a simple evidence folder, not on a six-account sightseeing tour the week before approval.

When they return to the market, they have the down payment, a documented closing fund, move-in cash and a reserve. They still need lender approval, an inspection and a legal review of the property. Their eventual purchase is less dramatic than the first open house and much more durable. The furnace has an age, the budget has walls and the first repair does not turn into high-interest debt.

blocks.text: Sophie and Marcus did not solve a larger target with last-minute debt. They adjusted price and time, documented the funds and kept a reserve beyond possession day.
The four-part target showed the missing costs. A longer timeline and a lower price kept the purchase from using up every dollar.
Sophie and Marcus found the real gap before a lender did, and chose a slower price over a faster credit card.
blocks.detail: Turning a target into a monthly transfer is what carried their fund the rest of the way without new debt.
blocks.extra: Turn your own target into a route next, one payday at a time.

sections.title: Turn the Target Into a Route

items.title: Set the complete target
items.text: Add the down payment, a researched closing-cost estimate, move-in needs and the reserve that must remain.

items.title: Subtract dedicated savings
items.text: Count money that is available and documented. Treat gifts, tax refunds or bonuses as assumptions until confirmed and permitted.

items.title: Calculate the gap
items.text: Divide what is left by the months until your target date, then turn the monthly figure into payday transfers.

items.title: Stress-test the household
items.text: Protect rent, debt payments, insurance, food and emergency needs. If the saving rate is fragile, change the price, target or date before using high-interest debt.

items.title: Prepare the evidence
items.text: Keep statements, FHSA or RRSP records, gift documents and explanations for large deposits. Ask the lender what proof is required and how recent it must be.

blocks.text: A down payment below 20% typically requires mortgage loan insurance. The insurance protects the lender, not the borrower, and its premium can increase the mortgage cost.
Provincial and city land-transfer taxes, registration charges, rebates and programs can change your closing cash a lot. Check the property’s location and the current rules before making an offer.

items.title: “If a lender approves the price, the home is affordable for my household.”
items.text: Approval only checks the lender’s rules. Affordability also includes repairs, utilities, property taxes, insurance, goals and the cash left after closing.

sections.title: Quick Check: Choose the Best Next Move

items.title: What is the current minimum down payment on an illustrative $550,000 home?
items.detail: $30,000: 5% of the first $500,000 plus 10% of the remaining $50,000.

items.title: Using FCAC’s range, what closing-cost band should be explored for $550,000?
items.detail: Approximately $8,250 to $22,000, before moving expenses and reserves.

items.title: Who does mortgage loan insurance primarily protect?
How do an FHSA and the HBP differ at a high level?
items.detail: An FHSA uses eligible contributions and qualifying withdrawals. The HBP lets you take eligible money out of RRSPs, and you generally repay it over time.

items.title: Why should an emergency reserve remain after possession?
items.detail: Repairs, income changes and other emergencies keep coming after you get the keys. Keeping cash on hand reduces the need for high-interest debt.

sections.title: Your Action: Home Purchase Cash Target

blocks.text: Use estimates until a property, province and lender are known. Do not record full account numbers, SINs, passwords or private tax identifiers in this workbook.
A ready home fund has four labelled jobs: purchase price, closing, move-in and resilience. The keys should not receive every dollar you own.
Save for the home purchase—not only the down payment.
blocks.detail: Build four separate funds, record where the money came from and pick a price and timeline that keep the household steady after you move in.

items.title: Down payment
items.text: Money you put directly toward the purchase price. The mortgage pays for the rest.

items.title: Closing costs
items.text: One-time costs of buying, such as legal fees, an inspection, tax adjustments, title insurance and transfer charges.

items.title: Mortgage loan insurance
items.text: Coverage that protects the lender when an insured mortgage borrower defaults.

items.title: FHSA
items.text: A registered plan for first-time home buyers who qualify. It has its own contribution, transfer and withdrawal rules.

items.title: Home Buyers’ Plan
items.text: A program that lets you take money out of your RRSPs to buy a qualifying home. You generally have to repay it.

items.title: Qualifying withdrawal
items.text: A withdrawal that meets the program’s rules on who qualifies, the home, the timing and the paperwork.

quiz.question: True or False: “Once I save the down payment, I am financially ready to buy.”

questions: Where do you want to buy, in what price range, and in which month?
What is the minimum down payment at your price, and how much do you want to save?
What do you expect to pay for closing costs, moving and first repairs? A range is fine.
How much emergency money will you keep after closing?
Which savings tools could you use: FHSA, HBP, TFSA, savings or GICs? What did you check about each one?
What is your total target and how much have you saved? What must you save each payday to close the gap, and when will you review it?
